paper_title: Can Visual Generation Expand What Unified Multimodal Models Know?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) receive image-generation supervision that exposes them to visual information not fully documented in text. Can learning to generate images expand what pretrained models know? We introduce Knowledge Transfer Probing (KTP), a controlled protocol that supplies new knowledge through image-generation training and tests its accessibility through text-only question answering. Across seven knowledge categories and three UMMs, we observe direct but uneven transfer from visual supervision to language. Motivated by these observations, we successively introduce Textual Alignment and Interleaved Image--Text Alignment, which connect generation and answering through shared knowledge and interleaved responses, respectively. Guidance on selected entities can improve knowledge access on other entities without QA supervision, with additional gains from interleaved alignment. Further analysis shows that knowledge correctly reproduced in images is often more accessible through text, although substantial gaps remain between the two forms of access. These findings support visual generation as a source of knowledge beyond textual supervision, and motivate joint investigation of training data design and model architecture to make this knowledge more broadly accessible.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: A key aspiration of unified multimodal models (UMMs) is to enable generation and understanding to reinforce one another, enabling more capable foundation models (Wu et al., 2026). This aspiration is particularly compelling because the visual world contains information that language does not fully document (Tong et al., 2026). photograph of local building or traditional artifact may reveal its structure, ornamentation, and spatial relationships, even when the accompanying caption mentions only its name or location. By learning to generate images, model receives supervision over visual content that need not be explicitly described in the accompanying text. Whether this learning also benefits understanding, however, remains an important question: can learning to generate images expand what unified models know? Knowledge sharing does not follow automatically from combining generation and understanding within one model. UMMs such as Janus-Pro and BAGEL report strong performance on separate visual understanding and generation benchmarks (Chen et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025). Tong et al. (2026) further demonstrates task-level benefits of multimodal co-training. These results, however, do not establish whether specific knowledge learned through generation becomes usable in language. Modal Aphasia highlights this distinction: unified models can reproduce learned visual concepts while struggling to describe them in words (Aerni et al., 2026). In this work, we study the language accessibility of visually acquired knowledge: The extent to which visual knowledge can be retrieved and correctly accessed and used in language. We develop Knowledge Transfer Probing (KTP), controlled protocol across seven visual knowledge categories, using fictional entityattribute associations to reduce interference from pretrained knowledge. During text-to-image (T2I) training, prompts identify entities and describe scenes, while target attribute values appear only in output images. We test transfer through text-to-text (T2T) QA that asks for an entitys attribute value without an input image. We experiment across UMMs with different architectures: BAGEL, SenseNova-U1 (Diao et al., 2026), and GLM-Omni. The results show that T2I training alone enables correct textual answers for some of this knowledge, demonstrating direct transfer from visual supervision to language. The extent of transfer varies across models and knowledge categories. Much of the knowledge correctly expressed in generated images remains absent from these initial answers. These results establish the potential of visual generation as source of knowledge. We further investigate whether auxiliary supervision during training can improve knowledge transfer. All entities receive T2I supervision, while subset also receives alignment examples. We compare two forms of training supervision: Textual Alignment provides text-only QA examples, whereas Interleaved ImageText Alignment combines image generation, visual observation, and answering in single response. The evaluation is conducted using the same T2T QA protocol on the remaining entities, whose target attribute values appear only in the T2I training images. Both forms of alignment improve textual answers for these entities, with interleaved alignment yielding larger gains. These results show that auxiliary supervision can improve access to knowledge beyond directly taught answers. The advantage of interleaved alignment further demonstrates that the organization of training supervision matters for knowledge transfer. Figure 1 summarizes our motivation and main findings. We will release the dataset and evaluation protocol. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce Knowledge Transfer Probing, controlled protocol to test whether visual generation expands what UMMs know. The protocol controls the source of target 2 knowledge and reduces interference from pretrained associations. It evaluates whether knowledge supplied through generation-training images becomes usable in text-only QA, taking first step toward measuring the knowledge contribution of visual generation. We demonstrate direct but incomplete knowledge transfer from visual generation to language. Across UMMs of varying architectures, generation supervision enables textonly answers for some knowledge, while much of the knowledge expressed in generated images remains absent from initial answers. Transfer varies substantially across models and knowledge categories. We show that targeted supervision improves knowledge access beyond directly supervised entities. Interleaved imagetext alignment yields larger gains than text-only alignment, establishing supervision design as an effective means of strengthening transfer. Together with the observed cross-model differences, these findings motivate joint investigation of architecture and data organization for knowledge sharing in UMMs.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Unified Multimodal Models. UMMs combine visual understanding and image generation. Chameleon and Emu3 autoregressively model discrete multimodal tokens (Team, 2025; Wang et al., 2024), while Transfusion, Show-o, and Show-o2 combine autoregressive text modeling with diffusion or flow matching for visual generation (Zhou et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025a;b). Janus-Pro, BAGEL, and SenseNova-U1 scale training and explore different designs for coupling these capabilities (Chen et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Diao et al., 2026). Controlled studies highlight visual-space alignment and architectural specialization as conditions for cross-task generalization and understanding-generation synergy (Zhang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). Cross-Modal Knowledge Transfer. Cross-modal knowledge transfer asks whether information learned through one modality or objective is accessible through another. Wen et al. (2025) report recall gaps under modality-specific training and mitigate them with in-distribution image-caption augmentation. Aerni et al. (2026) demonstrate modal aphasia: accurate visual reproduction after generation fine-tuning need not yield reliable verbal recall. Han et al. (2026) identify asymmetric, concept-dependent transfer between generation and visual question answering, and show that generative priors can accelerate supervised concept learning. UniKE examines whether textual knowledge edits affect generated images (Gao et al., 2026), while UReason studies alignment between textual reasoning and image generation (Yang et al., 2026b). We examine whether facts learned through image-generation training become accessible in textual question answering. Reasoning with Images. Images can serve as intermediate representations for reasoning. Visual Sketchpad uses drawing and vision tools (Hu et al., 2024), while DeepEyes learns active visual perception through reinforcement learning (Zheng et al., 2026). MVoT visualizes intermediate spatial states (Li et al., 2025), and Thinking with Generated Images interleaves image generation with visual subgoals and textual self-critique (Chern et al., 2025). Context Unrolling reasons across multiple modal representations (Yang et al., 2026a), while LatentUM performs interleaved cross-modal reasoning in shared semantic latent space (Jin et al., 2026). Following the visualization direction suggested by Aerni et al. (2026), we test whether generating intermediate images improves textual access to facts introduced through image-generation training.

sections.title: 3.1 TASK FORMULATION
sections.content: We investigate whether knowledge acquired through visual generation becomes accessible through language. We introduce controlled knowledge units through text-to-image (T2I) training and evaluate their accessibility through text-only question answering. Knowledge unit. We define knowledge unit as an entityattributevalue triplet τi = (ei, ai, vi), where ei denotes an entity, ai its target attribute, and vi the corresponding value. For example, Arvenbrocks jerseynumber10 describes fact that can be represented visually and expressed in 3 textual answer. To minimize the influence of the models pre-trained knowledge, we construct multiple fictional knowledge units that are absent from the model pre-training corpus and deliberately designed to deviate as much as possible from the pre-training distribution. Text-to-image supervision. We introduce the target knowledge through text-to-image (T2I) supervision. Each training example pairs text prompt with target image. The prompt identifies the entity and provides any necessary scene context but omits the target attribute value. The image depicts that value. For example, the prompt Generate an image of Arvenbrocks jersey is paired with an image of jersey bearing the number 10. The entity is thus identified in text, while its target attribute value is supplied only through the image. Textual accessibility. Our primary evaluation measures textual accessibility: whether the model can answer questions about the target knowledge without an input image. For each knowledge unit τi = (ei, ai, vi), we construct text-only question qi that identifies entity ei and asks for attribute ai, without revealing vi. For example, What number is on Arvenbrocks jersey? requires the answer 10. Let UMM(qi; T2T) denote the models textual response. We define textual accessibility over the knowledge set as Atext(UMM; K) =

sections.title: 3.2 DATA CONSTRUCTION
sections.content: We construct an image generation training dataset comprising seven tasks, grouped by the type of visual attribute associated with each knowledge unit: (1) object attributes and counts: color, count, and shape; (2) relative relationships: spatial and size; and (3) textual content: number and text. Figure 2 shows examples from all seven categories. Figure 2: Overview of the text-to-image dataset. Here we show examples from the seven visual knowledge categories. Each panel shows an entity, training image, and the target attribute value. For each task, we construct 50 knowledge units (triplets). Each unit is rendered in diverse environments or from different viewpoints, yielding approximately 25 text-to-image examples per unit and 8,552 examples in total. We follow three principles during data construction. Information isolation. We use language model to review the captions, ensuring that neither the captions nor the entity names directly reveal or indirectly suggest the target attribute value. Prior-free entities. All examples use entirely fictitious entity names in the fictional world MagicWorld to avoid relying on pretrained associations (e.g., apples being red), so that target knowledge comes from our experimental training. Balanced attributes. We approximately balance attribute-value distributions to mitigate implicit distributional biases.

sections.title: 3.3 MODELS AND TRAINING
sections.content: We study BAGEL (Deng et al., 2025), SenseNova-U1 (Diao et al., 2026), and an in-house GLMOmni model. BAGEL uses Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts (MoT) architecture with separate understanding and generation branches, together with semantic visual encoder and variational autoencoder. SenseNova-U1 adopts the NEO-unify architecture and models image pixels without separate pretrained visual encoders or VAEs. GLM-Omni is initialized from the pretrain base checkpoint of GLM-4.1V-Thinking (Team et al., 2026) and uses discrete image tokenizer based on X-Omni (Geng et al., 2025). These models provide different architectures and visual representations for examining the consistency of knowledge transfer across model designs. Training conditions. We compare three conditions. Direct transfer introduces target knowledge through T2I training without alignment supervision. Textual alignment adds text-only QA examples for alignment entities. Interleaved alignment further adds responses that combine image generation, visual observation, and textual answering. The latter two conditions use the same alignment entities and target attributes. Their data construction is described in Sections 4.2 and 4.3, respectively. To reduce the influence of response-format mismatch in the direct-transfer condition, we construct 10,000 text-only QA examples unrelated to the target knowledge. Their responses contain reasoning enclosed in <think> and </think> tags, followed by concise answer. These examples contain none of the target entities and provide no textual supervision for their attribute values.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENT AND ANALYSIS
sections.content: We first examine direct knowledge transfer under T2I training. Based on the observation, we then introduce auxiliary supervision on subset of entities to test whether guidance can improve knowledge access beyond directly taught answers. All three conditions use text-only QA at evaluation.

sections.title: 4.2 KNOWLEGE TRANSFER WITH TEXTUAL ALIGNMENT
sections.content: The preceding experiments show that learning target attribute value solely through image generation supervision offers limited benefits for textual question answering. We hypothesize that the entity attribute associations learned through generation may not yet be effectively linked to how the same 6 Figure 4: Overview of the KTP training and evaluation protocol. (a) Training: All entities receive T2I supervision, with target attribute values shown in images but omitted from captions. subset of entities additionally receives textual or interleaved imagetext alignment supervision. (b) Evaluation: For entities without alignment supervision, we measure textual accessibility through text-only QA and visual accessibility through image generation. attributes are expressed and accessed in textual question answering. We therefore introduce textual alignment supervision by providing both image generation data and textual questionanswer data for subset of entities. To avoid evaluation data contamination, we divide the entities in each task equally into two disjoint sets: an alignment entity set and test entity set. Figure 4 illustrates the supervision available to each set and the evaluation protocol. For each entity in the alignment entity set, we additionally construct 10 textual questionanswer examples , providing extra textual alignment supervision. Each question directly asks for the entitys target attribute, and each response consists of brief reasoning followed by final answer. Observation. The effect of textual alignment varies across models and categories  (Table 2)  . Mean textual accessibility improves for BAGEL and SenseNova-U1 but declines for GLM-Omni. Gains concentrate on shape and size, especially for SenseNova-U1, while other categories show mixed changes. Since test entities receive no QA supervision, these gains indicate that alignment can improve access to knowledge supplied only through images. However, all three models achieve 0% textual accessibility on number and text for test entities, compared with 72% and 7696%, respectively, for alignment entities. Thus, the ability to answer directly supervised questions does not extend to visually supplied values for other entities in these categories. Textual alignment connects generation and answering through shared entities and attributes but keeps them in separate training examples. We therefore examine whether linking image generation, visual observation, and answering within single response can strengthen this transfer.

Within single response, the model generates relevant image during reasoning, interprets its visual content, and uses it to continue reasoning and produce an answer. Questions follow the textual alignment format and directly ask for the entitys target attribute, with Please think with images. appended to each. Each response interleaves textual reasoning with one image that the model must generate as output, followed by final textual answer. The evaluation remains text-only, without input images or intermediate image generation. Observation. Averaged over the seven tasks, interleaved imagetext alignment improves text-only QA accuracy over textual alignment for all three models on the test entity set  (Table 2)  . Since target attributes for these entities are supplied only through image generation training, the gains show that interleaved supervision on other entities can improve textual access to visually acquired knowledge without directly teaching the test answers. Changes across individual tasks show that these benefits are uneven. GLM-Omni benefits most, particularly on shape (12% to 64%) and spatial (0% to 40%). At the same time, performance decreases slightly on some tasks. Interleaved image-text alignment therefore improves average performance in these experiments, but does not improve all tasks simultaneously. Further experiment 1: Which part of supervision contributes the most in interleaved image-text supervision? Interleaved imagetext alignment can further improve textual question answering on some tasks, but it remains unclear which supervision signals in the interleaved image-text data are primarily responsible for these improvements. We therefore conduct an ablation on GLM-Omni. We use the same interleaved image-text sequence for alignment, but mask the loss on the image portions of the interleaved alignment examples, while retaining supervision on their text portions. The textual alignment data and standalone image generation data remain unchanged, as do all other training and evaluation settings from the preceding section. Image-loss ablation in interleaved Figure 5: alignment on GLM-Omni. Masking the image loss retains the interleaved sequences and text supervision but substantially lowers performance. As shown in Figure 5, masking only the loss on the image portions of the interleaved examples reduces average text-only QA accuracy across the seven tasks on the test entities from 26.86% to 13.71%. The decline is concentrated in color, shape, and spatial. These differences indicate that the explicit image generation loss within interleaved sequences makes an important contribution to knowledge transfer. Integrating multiple task types (image generation, image understanding, and 8 textual reasoning) and multiple loss terms (image and text losses) within single training example offers more effective approach to enhancing models ability to transfer knowledge. Further experiment 2: Inference with visual CoT. To further investigate their potential for integrating generation and understanding, we evaluate the trained models by allowing them to recall visual content during reasoning. We refer to this procedure as visual chain-of-thought (Visual CoT). For models trained with interleaved image-text alignment, replacing direct textual answering with procedure that generates an image and then reasons with it can further improve average accuracy on the test entities  (Table 3)  . The improvement on number is particularly notable. All three models achieve 0% accuracy on this task when answering directly in text. With Visual CoT, their accuracies rise to 4%, 36%, and 20% for BAGEL, GLM-Omni, and SenseNova-U1, respectively. These results suggest that there remains considerable scope to further investigate knowledge transfer in UMMs. Table 3: Accuracy of text-only QA and Visual CoT (%). sections.title: 4.4 ASSOCIATION BETWEEN VISUAL AND TEXTUAL ACCESSIBILITY
sections.content: We examine whether knowledge correctly expressed in images is more likely to be retrieved through language. For each model and alignment condition, we pair generation and QA outcomes for individual knowledge units on the same test entities. Let and denote correct generated image and correct textual answer, respectively. Their association is measured by assoc = Pr(T I) Pr(T I), the difference in textual accuracy between successful and unsuccessful generation. The probes are evaluated separately; generated images are not provided during QA. Table 4 shows that visual and textual correctness are positively associated in most settings. Under textual alignment, the association is positive for BAGEL and SenseNova-U1 but negative for GLM-Omni; with interleaved alignment, it is positive for all three models. BAGELs association strengthens, while GLM-Omnis gap shifts from 11.28 to +8.09 percentage points. SenseNovaU1 retains the strongest association, although its gap decreases. Interleaved supervision therefore does not strengthen the association uniformly across models. Positive associations suggest that knowledge expressed through generation is often more accessible through language. Yet even with interleaved alignment, Pr(T I) remains below 50% for every model, leaving much of the knowledge reproduced in images absent from textual answers. These findings support the potential of learning from visual generation while highlighting the need for fuller and more consistent access through language. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Using the controlled protocol Knowledge Transfer Probing (KTP) across seven knowledge categories and three UMMs, we find that facts supplied only through image-generation targets can become accessible through text-only QA, though transfer remains limited and uneven. Alignment on selected entities can improve access on others, with interleaved alignment achieving higher mean accuracy than textual alignment in all three models. GLM-Omni ablation supports the contribution of image supervision within interleaved sequences, while Visual CoT further improves answering after interleaved training. These findings support visual generation as knowledge source beyond textual supervision. Future work should extend this study to natural visual data, isolate architectural effects, and investigate alignment data and inference strategies.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used AI tools to assist in implementing the data construction pipeline and used model APIs to generate data in batches. For experimental analysis, AI tools helped develop small analysis scripts, including those for computing and comparing conditional probabilities, and supported discussions of research ideas and experimental findings. During manuscript preparation, we used AI tools for translation and language editing. All AI-assisted writing was manually reviewed by the authors.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: In Appendix A.1, we describe the data construction pipeline, including image generation, editing, quality control, and the creation of captions and alignment data. In Appendix A.2, we summarize the data sampling ratios and training hyperparameters. Finally, in Appendix A.3, we specify the criteria for evaluating textual and visual accessibility, including answer matching and edit-distance thresholds.

sections.title: A EXPERIMENT DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 DATA CONSTRUCTION Table 5: The knowledge of entity, the range of attribute value, and image counts for the seven knowledge categories. Attribute Knowledge Value range Color The color of fictional font Count Shape Spatial Size Number Text Total The count of fictional collection The shape of fictional badge The stripe arrangement of fictional flag The larger country on fictional map The number of fictional persons jersey The title of fictional book blue, green, black, red, white, yellow 2, 3, 4, 5 circle, five-pointed star, pentagon, square, triangle 099 Images 1,226 1,195 1,248 1,220 1,218 1,244 1,201 8, We first use large language model (LLM) to construct 50 entityattributevalue triplets for each task. For each triplet, an image generation model produces base image depicting the entity with the specified attribute value. We then create 25 edited variants of the base image to diversify the scenes while aiming to preserve the entitys identity across samples. vision-language model (VLM) checks whether each image correctly depicts the target attribute and whether any confounding information has been introduced. Images that fail these checks are discarded. Table 5 reports the number of images retained for each task after quality filtering. Finally, we use VLM to generate captions from the retained images and construct two types of alignment data: textual alignment and interleaved imagetext alignment. Alignment data are constructed only for entities in the alignment set. A.2 TRAINING DETAILS Settings. For each condition, we train every model independently from its corresponding base checkpoint. We update the parameters used for understanding and generation with learning rate of 105. BAGEL and SenseNova-U1 use MSE and cross-entropy losses with weights 1 : 0.005 and 1 : 0.01, respectively. GLM-Omni uses unified token-level objective for text and image tokens. Data ratio. We observe that models learn visual information at different rates and fit alignment examples substantially faster than image generation examples. We therefore use different data sampling ratios for each model to reduce overfitting to the alignment data. Table 6 reports the ratios used when combining image generation, textual alignment, and interleaved imagetext alignment data. Table 6: Data sampling ratios when training with all three data sources. Model Image generation Textual alignment Interleaved alignment BAGEL GLM-Omni SenseNova-U1 0.956 0.990 0. 0.022 0.005 0.063 0.022 0.005 0.086 Hyperparameters. Table 7 lists the training hyperparameters for BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and GLM-Omni. 13 Table 7: Training hyperparameters for BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and GLM-Omni. Hyperparameter BAGEL SenseNova-U1 GLM-Omni Learning rate LR scheduler Weight decay Gradient clipping norm Warm-up steps Training steps Batch size 1.0 105 constant with linear warm-up 0 1.0 100 4000 8 1.0 105 constant 0 1.0 0 1500 1.0 105 constant with linear warm-up 0.1 1.0 100 1500 16 A.3 EVALUATION PROTOCOL Textual accessibility. We retain only the models final concise answer and compare it with the ground-truth answer, ignoring differences in capitalization and punctuation. Visual accessibility. We adapt the VLM quality checks used during data construction to evaluate generated images. For color, count, shape, and spatial, where images contain little or no text, we assess only whether the target attribute matches the ground truth. For size, number, and text, we additionally assess the text that must appear in the image. Specifically, size requires the two country names and their relative sizes to be correctly depicted; number requires the players name and jersey number; and text requires the book title. We apply an edit-distance tolerance to country names, player names, and book titles, while requiring jersey numbers to match the ground truth exactly. The maximum allowed edit distance depends on the length of the reference text. Let denote its length in characters. We define the threshold as δ(L) = 1, 5, 2, 3, > 10. 5 < 10, (4) text match is accepted when the edit distance between the rendered text and the reference does not exceed δ(L). This tolerance accommodates minor errors in rendered text and is intended to provide more faithful assessment of visual accessibility. A.4 QUALITATIVE EXAMPLES AND FAILURE ANALYSIS We examine individual test entities to compare visual reproduction, textual answering, and the effects of alignment and Visual CoT. All cases concern entities that receive image-generation supervision but no alignment supervision. Reference images are shown for illustration and are not provided during question answering. Figure 6: An example of an entity with visually accessible but textually inaccessible knowledge. Figure 6 shows shape example from the BAGEL evaluation in Section 4.3. Although the caption does not specify that the badge is triangular, the model generates badge with clearly defined 14 triangular shape, indicating visual accessibility of the target attribute. However, its textual answer is incorrect. This discrepancy illustrates gap between visual and textual accessibility: the model reproduces the attribute visually but fails to use that knowledge in textual question answering for this entity. The image caption of the example is: Could you make an illustration of Lomarras badge resting prominently on rustic, textured beige tablecloth within the MagicWorld. The scene is captured from close-up, eye-level perspective, highlighting the badges luxurious materials: deep, wine-red enameled face surrounded by gleaming, polished gold border. In the center of the crimson surface, delicate gold sigil composed of intersecting straight lines is meticulously inlaid. To the right of the artifact, small, earthy terracotta pot holds spiky green succulent, providing natural contrast to the metallic sheen of the badge. The background is softly blurred, showing sunlit room with white plates and hints of dark wooden furniture, creating warm, shallow-depth-of-field effect. The lighting is soft and natural, emphasizing the smooth, reflective texture of the enamel and the fine weave of the fabric beneath it. Figure 7: An example of an entity with textually inaccessible knowledge that becomes accessible with visual CoT. Figure 7 shows number example from the SenseNova-U1 evaluation in Section 4.3. The model fails to report the correct jersey number (31) in text-only evaluation. Under Visual CoT, it first generates an image that correctly depicts the target attributes and then obtains the correct answer by inspecting the image. This illustrates how visually accessible knowledge can support correct textual answers through image-assisted reasoning. The image caption of the example is: Generate scene showing the jersey of Dulmark as it hangs neatly over the back of deep blue velvet armchair within the MagicWorld universe. The perspective is direct view of the back of the teal-colored sports top, which is crafted from micro-perforated athletic mesh. The name DULMARK is printed in sharp, uppercase white typeface with black stroke, positioned above large, 15 stylized player number that occupies the center of the garment. The jerseys collar and sleeves are finished with classic white trim. Beside the chair on the light oak floorboards sits pair of vibrant teal footwear designed for the field. In the background, serene bedroom is illuminated by soft, diffused daylight streaming through window, with minimalist nightstand and comfortable bed adding to the lived-in feel. is bright and airy, creating high-fidelity, realistic art style that emphasizes the contrasting textures of the velvet, wood, and fabric.
